implementation_notes: Go's small standard library and fast-moving third-party ecosystem make layer accumulation common: `zap` in new packages and the standard `log` in old ones, `gin` in some handlers and `net/http` in others, `gorm` in one repository and `sqlx` in another. Go's advantage is that the compiler enforces the boundary, so a partially completed migration is still correct code — which is exactly why it persists. The detection is a per-capability package inventory (`go list -deps | ...` grouped by purpose) plus a grep for the legacy import; the enforcement is a lint rule forbidding the old import in new files, which is how Go projects actually finish migrations.
idiom_name: two logger packages, two config libraries, two router styles
pitfalls: A package imported by one file keeps the whole legacy library linked and available, so the migration cannot complete until that one file changes.
Two config libraries loaded from two sources means the effective configuration is the merge of both, which is a debugging nightmare.
Go's zero-cost migration to generics made some clone helpers unnecessary but they persist because removing them was never on any plan.
